blocks.prompt: Not an Insect
blocks.text: A spider is not an insect. An insect has six legs. A spider has eight. A spider makes silk inside its body. The silk starts out wet, like glue. It comes out of little taps at the back called spinnerets. When the spider pulls it, the wet silk turns into a dry thread. The spider builds a web out of the thread. Some parts of the web are sticky and some parts are not. The spider walks on the parts that are not sticky. That is how it does not get stuck in its own web.

blocks.prompt: How a Web Gets Built
blocks.text: An orb web looks simple. It is not. The spider starts by letting out a long thread and waiting for the wind to carry it across a gap. When the thread catches on the far side, the spider has a bridge. It walks the bridge, drops a line down the middle, and builds a frame. Then it lays the spokes, running out from the center like the spokes of a wheel. None of those spokes are sticky. Last comes the spiral. The spider walks around and around, laying a fresh line covered in tiny beads of glue. That is the part that holds the bug. When a moth hits the web, the spider does not run straight over to bite it. It waits. The web shivers, and the shivering tells the spider where the moth is and how big it is. Spiders cannot chew. A spider bites its meal, pumps in juices that turn the inside to soup, and drinks it. Many orb weavers take the whole web down at the end of the day and eat the silk, so they can spin it again tomorrow.

blocks.prompt: The Rope Inside the Spider
blocks.text: Every spider carries a rope factory in its abdomen. The rope is not stored as rope. It is stored as a thick liquid protein, packed into glands, and it stays liquid until the moment the spider needs it. When the spider pulls a thread out through its spinnerets, that liquid is squeezed down a narrow duct. Water is stripped out. The acid level changes. The long protein molecules, tangled and loose in the gland, are dragged into line and lock onto each other. Liquid goes in one end and solid thread comes out the other. No heat, no factory, no chemicals we would recognize. Just a spider, at room temperature, pulling. The thread it makes is remarkable. A spider's dragline, the safety line it trails behind it everywhere, is about as strong as steel of the same thickness, and steel is far heavier. Compare the two by weight and the silk wins easily. Better still, silk stretches before it breaks, so it soaks up energy instead of snapping. That combination, strong and stretchy at once, is what engineers chase and rarely catch. One spider does not make one silk. A garden orb weaver has several kinds of gland, and each makes a different thread: a tough dragline for the frame, a stretchy line coated in glue for the catching spiral, a soft wrapping silk for bundling prey, a papery silk for the egg sac. The spider chooses. It knows which tap to open. Here is a strange bonus. A spider has muscles to fold its legs but almost none to straighten them. It pushes its legs back out with fluid pressure, like a tiny hydraulic machine. That is why a dead spider curls up: the pressure is gone.

blocks.prompt: Flying Without Wings
blocks.text: In 1832, aboard the Beagle, a young Charles Darwin watched thousands of small red spiders land on the ship's rigging. The nearest land was sixty miles away. None of them had wings. What they had was silk. A spiderling that wants to leave home climbs to the highest point it can find, a fence post, a grass stem, a leaf tip. It stands on the very end, lifts its abdomen to the sky, and lets out several fine threads. Then it lets go. The threads catch the moving air and the spider is gone, sometimes a few yards, sometimes hundreds of miles. Pilots have collected spiders from the air more than two miles up. The behavior has a name that fits it perfectly: ballooning. For a long time everyone assumed the wind did all the work. The problem was that spiders balloon on days with almost no wind, and their threads fan apart in the air instead of tangling together, which is not what loose fibers normally do. In 2018 two researchers in Bristol tested a different idea. Earth carries a weak electric field, and the air above the ground is charged. Silk leaving a spider picks up a negative charge, and so does every thread beside it, which is why they spread: like charges push each other apart. The researchers put spiders in a sealed box with no wind at all and switched on an electric field. The spiders raised their front legs, tiptoed, and ballooned. Switch the field off and they came back down. So a spider can taste the electric state of the sky through the fine hairs on its legs, and decide that today is a good day to fly. This matters more than it sounds. Ballooning is how spiders reach islands, new fields, and burned ground within days. And there are a great many spiders to move. Two scientists added up the world's spiders in 2017 and estimated that they eat somewhere between four hundred and eight hundred million tons of insects every year, which is roughly what every human on Earth eats in meat and fish combined. The insects that would strip our crops are held down, in large part, by an animal that cannot fly, sailing across the sky on a thread it made out of itself.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Araneae, more than 50,000 known species
Dragline silk: steel's strength at a sixth of the weight
Spun from liquid protein, in water, at room temperature
Toughness beats Kevlar: strength times stretch

blocks.prompt: The Thread We Still Cannot Copy
blocks.text: Humans have farmed silk for roughly five thousand years, but never spider silk. The silk in a scarf comes from a caterpillar, Bombyx mori, which obligingly winds a single unbroken thread into a cocoon, and which will do it in trays, stacked, thousands to a room. Spiders will not cooperate. Put a thousand spiders in a room and you will return to a few fat spiders. They are predators, territorial, and perfectly willing to eat one another. That single fact has shaped a century of engineering. It has not stopped people from trying. Beginning in 2004, two men in Madagascar, Simon Peers and Nicholas Godley, set out to weave cloth from the silk of golden orb weavers. Teams of collectors gathered wild spiders each morning, held them in rows, drew the silk out by hand, and released them in the evening to be gathered again. Over about four years they used more than a million spiders. The result was a shimmering panel of naturally golden cloth, roughly eleven feet long, and the most expensive fabric ever made. It is beautiful, and it is a demonstration of the problem rather than a solution to it. The reason anyone bothers is that the material is genuinely extraordinary. A dragline thread, the line a spider trails behind itself as a safety rope, approaches the tensile strength of high grade steel while weighing about a sixth as much. Strength alone is not the interesting part, because Kevlar is strong too. Silk is also extensible: it can stretch by a third or more before it fails, and stretching is how a material swallows energy without breaking. Multiply strength by stretch and you get toughness, and by that measure dragline silk outperforms the fibers we manufacture, Kevlar included. A web is not a net. It is a shock absorber, built to catch an insect traveling at speed without flinging it straight back out. And the spider makes it out of nothing exotic, at room temperature, in water. The raw material is a protein solution stored in a gland as a thick liquid. As it is drawn down the duct, water is pulled out, the acidity rises, and shearing forces comb the tangled molecules into alignment, where they lock into tiny crystals bedded in a flexible matrix. The crystals supply strength. The matrix supplies stretch. The whole transformation happens inside a passage a few millimeters long, driven by nothing more than the pull of the spider's own leg. Our strongest fibers are made the opposite way: high heat, high pressure, harsh solvents, and enormous energy bills. So laboratories skipped the spider. They put spider silk genes into bacteria, into yeast, into silkworms, and famously into goats, whose milk then carried silk protein that could be filtered out and spun. Every attempt produces the protein. Every attempt struggles at the same step, which is the spinning. It turns out the recipe was never only the protein. It was also the duct, the water, the acid, the speed, and the pull. A spider is not a bag of silk. It is a machine for making silk, and the machine is the part we have not copied.
